subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF AMENDMENT TO REGULATIONS
ANNOUNCEMENT OF AMENDMENT TO REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to inform the house of an amendment to the regulations regarding acreage payments to western grain producers.
An order in council of August 31, 1960 authorized the payment of $1 per acre to a maximum of 200 acres to holders of wheat board permits for the 1959-60 crop year. The use of the 1959-60 permits as a basis of payment permitted the payments to be made much more promptly than would have been the case if the 1960-61 permits had been used with the resultant delays pending the issue of the new permits. The main issue of the payment cheques was completed on October
7.	The value of cheques issued to date is $40,070,000.
Because of the early snows and other climatic conditions in 1959 a considerable number of grain producers, who normally produce grain for market, did not take out delivery permits. It was felt that such producers should obtain the benefits under this program. The amendment to the regulations now makes farmers eligible for payments if they held wheat board permits in 1958 and 1960 and if they were actual grain producers in 1959. To qualify they will be required to complete an affidavit giving details of their operations. Applications are being prepared and will go out shortly. To qualify for the payment these applications must be returned to the Canadian wheat board, as agent of the minister, by February 28, 1961.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF AMENDMENT TO REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not expect that the announcement just made by the Minister of Agriculture will mean any great additional burden on the treasury, but it will make it possible for a number of producers, who are not otherwise able to qualify, to obtain the $1 an acre payment.
I noticed that the minister made the factual statement that payment was made on the 1959-60 permit books, and he went on to say this had been done because it would expedite the payment and made it possible
for the payments to be made more quickly.
I hope, I expect and I am confident that there is also another reason not mentioned by the minister, namely that the agricultural producers can look forward to receiving that much, if not more, on the 1960-61 permit books, and that by paying them on 1959-60 permit books the government is in fact, although it has not yet announced it, putting this before the country as a minimum annual payment.

subtopic: THREATENED RAIL STRIKE

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: THREATENED RAIL STRIKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it would be fitting that I should bring the house up to date with regard to the discussions that have taken place in the last couple of days in connection with the dispute between the non-operating unions and the two railways.
As I said the other day, with a view to bringing the two parties together, a week ago Saturday in the city of Montreal the Minister of Labour, the Minister of Transport and the Postmaster General met with the representatives of the labour unions and thereafter with the presidents of the two railways. On that occasion there was a general discussion of the subject, following which a letter was received by the three ministers in question from Mr. F. H. Hall, vice grand president of the brotherhood of railway and steamship clerks and chairman of the negotiating committee.
I have the letter before me, and I will merely refer to part of it unless the house wishes me to read it in full. In part it states:
On behalf of the negotiating committee of the unions... I have to tell you that following the discussion of last Saturday we have not been able to reach a conclusion which, in light of the mandate that we have from the employees, would permit us to comply with your request for postponement of the strike date of December 3.
Then various facts are set out. At that time the request was, in view of the hardship that would be created and the economic dislocation that would follow, that an agreement might be arrived at, without sacrifice of their rights in any way on the part of either the unions or the railway companies, to postpone the strike, or action in that regard, until the
240	HOUSE OF
Statement on Threatened Rail Strike government would have had the opportunity of securing the report of the royal commission on transportation.
At that time it was asked as to when that report would be forthcoming. I then got in touch with Mr. MacPherson, the chairman, and he advised that although every effort had been made to accelerate the termination of the work of the commission it had been proven impossible, with the various representations being made and those in anticipation, to hold out any hope of a report containing recommendations before March 31, 1961.
You will recall, sir, that one reason for setting up the royal commission, amongst others, and most important, was to assure that a reasonable degree of equality of opportunity would be given to Canadians in all parts of Canada whatever their geographical address. Over the years discriminatory rates had developed which prevented various areas in Canada from being able to compete on an equitable basis. The horizontal increases in freight rates since 1945 amounting to more than 145 per cent, would have the effect of increasing discrimination wherever it existed.
However, following the meeting, and after my conversation with Mr. MacPherson, the Minister of Labour communicated with Mr. Hall, the chairman of the negotiating committee of the unions, and informed him and the committee when the report would be received. It was subsequent to this, on November 21, that Mr. Hall wrote these three ministers the letter to which I have already made reference.
During the week it was decided that one negative answer to the suggestion, which we thought was a reasonable one, was not enough, and that we ought to continue to do everything we could to bring about a settlement of the dispute to the end that a strike would be avoided. As a result, on Saturday I joined my three colleagues in meeting first with Mr. Hall and the 14 representatives of the unions concerned, and thereafter with the presidents of the two railways.
I pointed out the disorder and economic chaos which would result, in particular in grain, livestock and industrial production, and I think that is a fair description of the result of a strike at this time. After outlining the matter in some detail I pointed out that the recommendation of the board of conciliation had no binding effect. In 1950 it was the union that refused to accept the recommendation of the board of conciliation, and on this occasion it was the railway companies that were taking the same attitude. I also dealt with the costs of the recommendations, which provided for a 2-cent increase


per hour on January 1, 1960 and a 5-cent increase per hour on September 1, 1960, as well as certain other vacation rights, the total cost of which for the year 1960 would amount to $6,947,000; and that from January to June in 1961 the total further cost, for the period of six months until the report and recommendation of the royal commission had been handed down, would amount to a further $6,086,000 or a total of some $13,033,000.
I can say that the meeting with the union representatives was conducted in an amicable way, as I would expect from representatives of the railway workers who are at all times good citizens and most law abiding and reasonable in their representations. I pointed out that many telegrams had been received by me, which I had before me, and that they came from all parts of Canada and all the various economic units in Canada such as, for example, representatives of the agricultural industry in the highest echelons, livestock producing organizations, fruit organizations, business in general and indeed representatives of most of the economic sectors of Canada. Mr. Hall said he had also received many telegrams supporting the stand he was taking as chairman of the union. I asked him the following questions after discussion.
1.	Is your decision final and absolute that there shall be a strike unless the pay recommendations of the conciliation board are met before 8 a.m., December 3? His answer was yes.
2.	Would you be prepared to postpone any strike action until May 15, 1961 provided that in doing so there would be no prejudice in connection with collective bargaining processes and your right to claim for wage increases as recommended by the conciliation board, the first to commence on January 1, 1960 and the further one recommended for September 1, 1960?
I said that any acceptance of this request for a postponement was made on the basis that we did not intend to give a subsidy from the people of Canada, for in doing so we would simply be placing on the people of Canada as a whole a responsibility which at this time did not rest upon the people as a whole. I said that when the freeze was lifted on the increase of freight rates, which was imposed at about the time of the setting up of the royal commission, the union and the companies would be in a position to bargain again and, I repeat, without prejudice to the right of the union, on any request to go back to January 1, 1960.
The answer was no. He said that to do so would be to prejudice the employees and would be destructive of their morale, and that in any event, while the majority conciliation

Statement on Threatened Rail Strike
report had been accepted, it was felt that the amount recommended was too small.
In company with my colleagues I then met with the railway presidents, and I received the same type of reply in so far as the question was concerned: Is your decision final that you will not accept the recommendations of the majority of the conciliation board? The answer was that they would not, and they gave the reasons which have already been given public notice for a considerable period of time.
The government intends to exhaust every avenue with a view to securing an agreed settlement of this dispute, and because of that fact a further meeting has been called for today. Although the discussions on Saturday indicated no probability of settlement, I have found through the years that continued meetings oftentimes do achieve a measure of agreement, even though the parties to it start out each firmly convinced that there will be no alteration in their viewpoint.
I shall again today-my colleagues with me-meet with both the representatives of the unions and the representatives of the companies. On this occasion we shall meet together. I shall be there at the opening, and after a preliminary survey my colleagues will remain and further endeavour will be made to bring about a settlement which will be acceptable and will avoid the serious if not tragic results of a strike.
A strike at this time will bring hardship to Canadian producers. It will affect livestock, grain, industrial production and the like. It will shortly have the same effect on consumers, as available stocks are used up. It will mean that thousands of persons unconnected with the railroads will be out of work. A strike at this juncture-and I have emphasized this most definitely-could not but have a serious and adverse effect on Canada's export trade. It would affect, as well, that trade which in the ordinary run of things may be expected in the busy Christmas season.
I am not here to place before the house the merits or demerits of the stand taken by either side, but I am here to point out the seriousness of the situation and, I believe, the reasonableness of the request. The suggestion is to wait until May next, the date fixed, at which time we will have the report of the royal commission.
There are only two ways in which these extra amounts can be paid. One is by subsidy and the other is by increased freight rates. Increased freight rates are prevented because of the freeze. In order to assure that the union shall not suffer as a result of the
freeze, I repeat once more that the offer without any guarantee attached to it is that they shall be in no way prejudiced.
I hope, sir, that as always good sense will prevail and that out of the meeting this afternoon a settlement will result-although I do not express any hope on the basis of the discussions that have already taken place -which will prevent a strike which in my opinion the Canadian people do not want at this time.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: THREATENED RAIL STRIKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the house and the country will be grateful to the Prime Minister for the statement he has just made, as well as for the attempt which he and his colleagues have made on Saturday and will again make this afternoon at four o'clock in the hope of averting a national strike, although I must say immediately that it is unfortunate that these attempts were not undertaken some time earlier. However, I will not press that point at this time, other than to say that those of us who sit on this side of the house, as I am sure all members do, appreciate the great importance for our economy at this time to maintain railway service in Canada. A railway strike would have tragic consequences, especially at this period when we have mounting unemployment. We are therefore facing a most serious situation which must be considered by all of us objectively and responsibly.
When negotiations between the unions and the railways failed to produce a settlement a conciliation board was established to look into the dispute and make recommendations. The board was chaired by Mr. Justice Mil-vain, an appointee of the present government. The majority report, as the Prime Minister has already indicated, recommended a wage increase in three stages: 2 cents in January of 1960, 5 cents in September of the same year, and 4 per cent or the equivalent of 7 cents on May 1, 1961. According to reliable estimates this would cost the railways about $6.9 million in 1960. Fifty per cent of the total increase recommended would become due only on May 1, 1961.
Under the circumstances it seems to us the government does not have any alternative but to propose a settlement on the basis of the majority report. It certainly cannot question the competence of the board, since it chose and appointed the chairman. Moreover, the board held a long series of meetings and heard evidence from qualified experts representing both parties. The board took considerable time hearing the evidence, and the submissions made to the board both by the non-operating unions and the representatives of the two railways. The board handed down

Statement on Threatened Rail Strike its decision after careful consideration. I think it can safely be said that the government cannot challenge the competence of the board.
In addition, as I understand it, the award of the conciliation board would not impose an intolerable financial burden on the companies or the government in 1960 and the first four months of 1961.
I listened with care to what the Prime Minister had to say about the two questions which he put to the representatives of the non-operating unions, when he inquired about their willingness to postpone the strike until after the royal commission on transportation had handed down its report. At this juncture I should like to bring this fact to the attention of the Prime Minister. When the responsible members of the non-operating unions made representations with reference to this very matter before the royal commission on transportation they were told by the former chairman of that commission, and rightly so, that this was a matter they could not discuss or take up with them because it was already before a board of conciliation, and under their terms of reference they had no jurisdiction to consider the representations.
The Prime Minister has now asked the unions to wait until the royal commission has handed down its report. The Prime Minister knows, as he himself has indicated in this house before, that sometimes a royal commission of this importance and this nature is not always able to hand down a report within the time the government expects. Perhaps the hon. gentleman will remember that when he announced the establishment of this commission he said to the house that it would hand down its report by a certain date. That was not possible due to circumstances over which the government nor anybody else had any control, and I am not finding any fault with that. The point is, however, that the government had to bring down legislation to meet the position pending the final report of the royal commission.
When the Prime Minister indicated that after March 31 the government would have had a month to consider the recommendations of the royal commission on transportation and would therefore be in a position to propose financial assistance, if necessary, to the railways in order to enable them to meet their obligations, I am not challenging that remark, of course, but I do bring to the attention of the Prime Minister the facts that existed when he himself announced the appointment of the royal commission.
It seems to us that it would be unwise to postpone the final settlement of the present dispute until the commission has presented its report, because the commission would


not then be in a position to take that important factor into consideration in making its recommendations.
In the light of all those circumstances there is only one fair solution to the present emergency, and that is the implementation of the majority report of the conciliation board.

subtopic: THREATENED RAIL STRIKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has made an important statement on this vital subject this afternoon. I think we are all in agreement on one particular aspect of the question, namely the great hardship that would follow from a railway strike to many sections of the country. Everything that is possible and feasible should be done to bring about an agreed settlement. I express the hope that the Prime Minister and those who will be participating in the discussions may be successful in that regard.
The question is whether the workers at this time are to be given a settlement based on the majority report of the conciliation board. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, there is the belief abroad that railway wages in general are among the cream of wages in this country. I do not think that is correct. As a matter of fact in recent years, in a relative sense when compared with certain other industries, payments obtained by railway workers have been going down.
The case put forward by the majority conciliation board report is that while they are not able to recommend at this time full parity of railway wages with the durable goods industry, they are recommending an association between those two industries; they are recommending certain increases so that the disparity, the difference, will not be broadened. The recommendations, as the hon. member for Laurier has already spelled out, are 2 cents an hour retroactive to January 1 of this year, 5 cents an hour effective September 1 and a further 7 cents an hour on May 1, 1961; and four weeks' holidays sifter 25 years.
The Prime Minister has said that there are two ways in which this recommendation may be met. The first is to provide the sum of money involved through increases in freight rates; the second is by way of a government subsidy. I suggest to him that there is a third way, namely, that of the companies, in the normal course of events, paying this money out of their own funds. I suggest further that from all indications the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, which is usually considered the yardstick, certainly as far as freight rates are concerned, is in a position to make such a payment. I am merely pointing out to the Prime Minister that there is a third method by which those payments can be made.

Statement on Threatened Rail Strike
I am hopeful that as a result of the negotiations that take place a settlement can be reached and a strike can be avoided. I welcome the fact that in the Prime Minister's statement this afternoon there was no threat, there was no suggestion of compulsory arbitration. I think compulsory arbitration is undemocratic, is not in keeping with our concept of freedom in this country, and should be resorted to only in case of the severest national emergency. I am suggesting that compulsory arbitration in this situation should not only be avoided but is not in any way necessary.
Reports have it that a great many millions of dollars are involved. I have seen newspaper reports that estimate that it would cost something like $39 million a year to fulfil the recommendations of the conciliation board. I am pleased that the Prime Minister placed on record the amount of money involved in those various categories, and that to bring about the necessary increase in wages would take some $13 million between now and the end of June next. I do not feel that the Prime Minister should say to the workers that they should forgo any benefits that would result from the implementation of the majority report. After all, when the royal commission began its sittings this question of dealing with labour matters was raised, and the royal commission was opposed to and rejected any inquiry into this situation.
The Prime Minister has told us he expected that in the normal course of events the royal commission report would have been tabled before now. Although he has been pressing the royal commission to make its report at an early date, the commission has told him that it will not be able to report until the end of March. I do not think the Prime Minister is justified in asking the railway workers to forgo the benefits that would result from the implementation of the majority report merely because the royal commission established by the government has been so long delayed in bringing in its report. I suggest that if this is the only alternative, the government should be prepared to consider an interim subsidy of the amount the Prime Minister mentioned, which would carry this situation up to and beyond the report of the royal commission. I think by this means the workers would receive the benefits from the majority report and the government's policy of preventing any further increases in freight rates at this time would be fulfilled, and the country and parliament would have a chance to look at the report of the royal commission when it is tabled.
I hope that in the spirit the Prime Minister referred to the railway workers this afternoon, following his statement that he intends to exhaust every avenue for an agreed settlement, his efforts in this regard will be successful.

speechtext: No. On a point of order, I think the Prime Minister misunderstood what I did say, or perhaps I did not make myself clear; let me put it that way. subtopic: THREATENED RAIL STRIKE
speechtext:
As a statement of fact by the hon. gentleman that is correct, but he misconceives the nature of the statement I made earlier. The royal commission was set up for the purpose of bringing about an equalization of opportunity in this country by making recommendations that would remove the anomalous condition that prevails today when some parts of our country are subject to discriminatory rates. Now, naturally, it would be impossible to have any evidence given on the part of the unions. Their representations were made to a board of conciliation which, of course, has no binding effect whatsoever.
What we are asking is simply this. Instead of bringing in other means which we agree

Proposed Legislation
could be applicable to the circumstances, namely an increase in freight rates, in order to enable the railways to make payment of the increased amounts provided for in the recommendations of the conciliation board, the unions, without prejudice in any way, should wait until parliament will be in a position to act. I give the undertaking that on or before May 15, parliament will be in a position to bring about, through legislation, the recommendations showing the necessity and efficacy of that course being followed, to remove discrimination and at the same time enable the railway companies to operate.
The hon. member for Assiniboia says "They can pay". The C.N.R.'s deficit this year is estimated to be around $75 million. The hon. member for Assiniboia referred to the figures which I gave showing the cost up to June 30. Comparing the cost for 1960 and 1961, the increase would be some $44,207,000, of which a very considerable amount would be payable by Canadian National Railways. To indicate the division, in 1961 the Canadian National's share of the expenditure would be approximately $19,500,000 and for 1960 the amount would be a total of $6,947,000. I rose simply to bring into proper perspective what I believe to be a misconception on the part of the hon. member.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR REGULATION OF EXTRAPROVINCIAL TRUCKING
PROVISION FOR REGULATION OF EXTRAPROVINCIAL TRUCKING
speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-44, to regulate extraprovincial transport.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR REGULATION OF EXTRAPROVINCIAL TRUCKING
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR REGULATION OF EXTRAPROVINCIAL TRUCKING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of the bill is to provide for the regulation of the extraprovincial trucking industry in order to obtain the maximum public benefit from a truly competitive enterprise system. The policy is based upon control of entry into the extraprovincial trucking industry by the licensing of services and the control of tariffs. This control of licensing and tariff is to be exercised by a federal regulatory mechanism which is referred to in the bill as a joint transport board. This board is constituted, as occasion may require, by members from the transport boards of those provinces which have an interest in an extraprovincial licence application.
The joint transport board determines whether a licence shall issue and, if issued, sets the tariff for the service. The board weighs its actions on the scale of public convenience and necessity. Its members, as members of the provincial boards, are experienced in applying the public interest to the practical necessities of the trucking industry. Federal control over and guidance of the joint transport board in the national public interest is provided through regulation by the governor in council.
The bill provides for the repeal of the Motor Vehicle Transport Act, which is the present federal regulatory control.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: STATEMENT ON REPORTED INCREASE IN U.S. VALUATIONS FOR DUTY
speechtext:
Last Friday morning, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Laurier asked for my comments on a press report to the effect that the United States bureau of customs has increased in an arbitrary way the valuation for duty purposes of Canadian goods in contravention of the 1956 agreement on firm valuations, and that the Canadian case had been presented too ineffectually and with too little authority.
I have now seen the press report to which the hon. member referred'. I am glad to have this opportunity not only to correct the erroneous impression apparently held by certain sections of the press that a United States customs accommodation is, in fact, an agreement between our two governments, but also to assure the house that what my hon. friend describes as the "Canadian case" was appropriately presented.
I have here a lengthy statement setting forth the details of this arrangement. Rather than


take up the time of the house I would ask for unanimous consent to place this statement on the record.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: STATEMENT ON REPORTED INCREASE IN U.S. VALUATIONS FOR DUTY
speechtext: No objection, providing it is not a political statement.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON REPORTED INCREASE IN U.S. VALUATIONS FOR DUTY
speechtext: Never a political statement; just the facts.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: STATEMENT ON REPORTED INCREASE IN U.S. VALUATIONS FOR DUTY
speechtext: Does the minister have unanimous consent to have the residue of his statement printed in the record at this point as though it had been read.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON REPORTED INCREASE IN U.S. VALUATIONS FOR DUTY
speechtext:
Agreed.
[Editor's note: The statement above referred to is as follows:]
In 1956, in order to accommodate Canadian exporters, the United States bureau of customs set up a procedure by which Canadian exporters might obtain, before shipment, an advisory opinion on the value for duty that U.S. customs was likely to set on their entries. This was an accommodation procedure set up by the bureau of customs for the convenience of Canadian exporters, and should not be confused with an agreement between the two governments. When this procedure was adopted it was made clear that opinions applied for would be advisory only; the bureau could not be bound prior to actual entry and appraisement.
Previously, both exporters and U.S. importers had long been troubled by uncertainty regarding the valuation on which U.S. duties would be levied. Not infrequently value, for duty purposes, was appraised on 'foreign' value which was higher than either shipper or consignee had anticipated, and required, therefore, the deposit of additional duties. The new accommodation procedure was widely welcomed, and worked satisfactorily up until shortly after the 28th February, 1958, when the new value for duty provisions of the Customs Simplification Act of 1956 took effect.
These new provisions of the U.S. customs law eliminated, in most cases, the concept of 'foreign value' in appraisement of the value of goods for duty purposes, and substituted in its place the concept of 'export value'.
Without going into the detail of the definitions in the law regarding 'export value', it is enough to note that a key definition is '... freely sold... or offered for sale', and that this means 'at a price which fairly reflects the market value of the merchandise'.
In 1958 certain Canadian companies, all subsidiaries, obtained advisory opinions as to the value for duty of certain shipments of components they proposed to ship exclusively to their parent corporations in the United States. Possibly because of the new law's

novelty and the lack of experience with it of the U.S. customs appraisers at the border, they were advised that these goods would be appraised on the basis of 'export value'.
It was not until about a year later that the bureau of customs attorneys concerned with valuation principles came to a review of these cases. They concluded that because these companies' prices for shipments to their parents did not fairly reflect the market value of the goods in Canada-as prescribed by the U.S. valuation law-'export value' did not, therefore, exist.
The bureau accordingly ruled that valuation in the case of shipments made exclusively to parent companies must-lacking a finding of both 'export value', and the prescribed alternative 'United States value'-be based on 'constructed value'. 'Constructed value' is the cost of materials and fabrication plus an addition for general expenses and profit.
This, in effect, reversed the previous customs opinions on which these companies had shipped and put the value for duty in these particular cases back up to roughly their list price in Canada to Canadian purchasers.
The grievance of these exporters was brought to the attention of the Department of Trade and Commerce by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, and the government sought clarification of the matter in Washington. After a most careful review of the problem the American authorities replied that the bureau ruling complained of was, under the law as it now stands, the only ruling possible.
The press accounts referred to have greatly exaggerated this issue, and have implied that the bureau of customs has shown bad faith. This is not the case. U.S. valuation law is complex and its technical points are not always readily grasped by persons unfamiliar with it.
It is not true, as some accounts have seemed to represent, that Canadian exporters are denied valuation on the more liberal terms of the new 'export value'. Any Canadian firm-if it ships to more than one unrelated purchaser in the United States, in the ordinary course of trade-can have its export price accepted as the 'export value' for duty purposes. The limit to which the exporter may lower his price for sale to the United States is set only by the U.S. anti-dumping law, the application of which in the past 10 years, and particularly since its recent modification, cannot be described as unduly severe.
To date scarcely more than a half dozen subsidiaries of U.S. companies have been involved in this valuation problem. It would indeed be unfortunate were this problem permitted to be so distorted as to create general difficulties in relation to United States
Inquiries of the Ministry valuation practices. The new valuation procedure, far from being an obstacle, represents a major improvement in Canadian access to the U.S. market.
The problem which arises in exclusive transactions between related companies where there is, in fact, no other possible buyer, is difficult, and is receiving attention. We know of only a very few such cases.
In all the others the solution to the problem is already in the hands of the companies and their parents if they choose to use it.

speechtext: I wish to direct a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare, of which I have given notice. speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Monleilh (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO DISPOSAL OF U.S. ATOMIC WASTES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the hon. member's interest in this subject, and I am glad to be able to assure him that disposals at the site mentioned would not seem to constitute a contamination hazard to Nova Scotia.
The United States atomic energy commission has licensed two companies to dispose of low level packaged wastes in an area in international waters where the minimum depth is 1,000 fathoms. This area, which I find is just over 150 miles south of Yarmouth, was selected by the commission following consultation with the competent scientific groups in the United States.
The wastes are mixed into concrete and encased in steel drums before disposal, which usually is made in other areas further south. The two firms were licensed over 2 years ago, but no disposals on their part have yet been reported in this particular area, although the commission dumped small quantities of low level wastes there prior to that time.
For a statement of Canada's position on radioactive waste disposals in areas of this kind I would refer to a reply made by the Prime Minister to a more general question on the subject, on July 13 of this year. The answer may be found on page 6173 of Hansard. Reference is made there to an ad hoc panel appointed by the international atomic energy agency. The panel, which included a Canadian representative, presented the findings I referred to in the house on November 18. It recommended that disposal sites, once designated, should be monitored regularly and that a registry should be kept of all disposals. The United States atomic energy commission is adhering to these recommendations to my department's satisfaction.


It is worth stressing that a number of investigations into waste disposal methods have been conducted, and that none of these reported that any contamination had been detected, even in an area where very substantial disposals were made.

He said: Mr. Speaker, there was a wide discussion of this measure at the resolution stage, and I think my remarks today can be very brief in consequence. I should like to acknowledge the support that this measure received in all parts of the house at the resolution stage, and to thank hon. members for the approval of the measure which they then expressed.
There has been, in the meantime, an opportunity for the public to examine the measure, and for representatives of the organizations of retail business and other businesses which will be principally concerned in the measure to do likewise; and we have had further opportunities for consultation with the banks. The measure has been received not only favourably but enthusiastically by the representatives of retail merchants, and we have received further assurances of co-operation on behalf of the chartered banks.
Sir, at this stage we are considering the principle of this measure. I think the nature of the measure is such that the principle may be described in this form, that government guarantees should be provided for loans by banks to the classes of small business named in the bill in order to extend intermediate term credit to these businesses for the purpose of financing their capital improvements.
The house is well aware of the definition that has been given to small business in the measure. It is not easy, Mr. Speaker, to devise an adequate definition of small business that will meet all circumstances. The definition that has been written into this bill is, I think, placed upon the only footing that could be regarded as satisfactory for this purpose, namely gross revenue.
I think the house will be interested to know what percentage of businesses in the four categories we calculate will qualify under the definition of small business. Based upon the 1951 census and upon a study that was made by the dominion bureau of statistics in 1957, our calculation-and these figures can only be approximate-is that 92 per cent of the business establishments in Canada in the four categories of business enumerated in the bill will qualify for loans under the terms of the measure.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF LOANS TO SMALL BUSINESS ENTERPRISES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we of the official opposition support the principle of this bill, as we did that of the resolution which preceded it. As emphasized by our leader, we Liberals are anxious to facilitate whatever legislation the government puts forward to deal with the problem of unemployment and the economic emergency which faces us at this time. We are anxious to get something done. It was for that reason that we deliberately refrained from putting up more than one speaker at the resolution stage. Though we may not restrict ourselves to the same degree on second reading, nevertheless for the same reasons I shall endeavour to make my remarks as brief as possible.
At the resolution stage we were concerned mainly with the general principle of providing loans to small businessmen. Now on second reading we have the bill before us and we can therefore see how the general principle has been applied and assess its value in the light of the most urgent needs of small businessmen.
The four most urgent needs of small business today are (1) credit, including both long term and medium term credit; (2) low rates of interest; (3) tax relief, and (4) working capital. How does the bill meet those four needs? It makes no provision whatsoever for working capital. We can understand the emphasis which the bill places on building premises and equipment because we know the minister and the government are looking upon it in terms of providing employment. But lack of working capital is often one of the greatest obstacles to expansion of small business, and it is one need which has to be met before any solution of a permanent nature can be evolved.
This bill does not give any measure of tax relief. Tax relief was one of the main features of the Pearson plan which I put on the record the other day, and which can be found on page 57 of Hansard of November 21. This proposal was ridiculed by members opposite, but it is interesting to note that the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, in its policy declarations of 1960-61, has referred to the need for relief from the tax burden. For example, I quote from page 33 of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce policy declarations:
The chamber is firmly of the opinion that the burden of taxation is too onerous in Canada, that personal and corporate income tax rates discourage


initiative, and that sales and similar taxes add appreciably to the costs of domestic producers and to consumer prices.
Perhaps this particular bill would not be an appropriate measure in which to make tax changes, but we do hope that the minister will keep this in mind when he brings in his so-called baby budget, which we hope will be introduced before this house rises for the Christmas recess.
With regard to the need for low interest rates, as far as we can see the rate on these loans will be the normal bank rate of 6 per cent.

Will the government guarantee be interpreted as lessening the risk, therefore requiring less collateral? Will the loans be extended to borderline risks which otherwise might be rejected?

Mr. Speaker, I have a comment or two to make at this stage on this particular bill. We all know that the type of economy we have, which is agreeable to the Minister of Finance and his colleagues, from time to time places certain groups in our economy at a disadvantage visa-vis other groups, and that the policy of the C.C.F. and the democratic socialist movement has always been to lessen this disadvantage as much as possible and make sure that so long as we have a capitalistic type of economy, all sections of that economy are able to function within it to the best advantage.
Unfortunately, small businessmen are one group which has been at a particular disadvantage for a variety of reasons. This bill

Guarantee of Loans to Small Businesses
as a half measure will somewhat alleviate the squeeze and the disadvantage which small businessmen have found themselves in over the years. It is unfortunate, though, that even although the party to which my friend the Minister of Finance belongs, before it became the government, espoused this idea of assistance to small business, it took the economic conditions that we have today to force him and his colleagues to introduce a measure such as this when a similar proposal, or an expansion of it, could easily have been introduced two or three years ago, which perhaps would have assisted some of the small businessmen, or prevented them from getting caught in the economic squeeze in which they find themselves to a great extent because of other activities of my hon. friend and his government.
I would have thought, Mr. Speaker, that it would have been advantageous to agree to have this particular bill referred to the banking and commerce committee when it is established, which I hope will be soon, in order that a complete and full examination could be made by the committee. If that were done the people who are interested in it could make their views known to the committee rather than through the narrow conduit pipe to the minister's office, and also we could have before the committee the views of the Department of Trade and Commerce or its small business bureau. If this bill were sent to that committee we could get the ideas of the small business bureau-if that is the proper designation of the division-with respect to this particular piece of legislation.
Our examination of the bill certainly indicates to us that it leaves much to be desired, and that a number of improvements could be made in the bill itself. Having in mind, sir, the speeches made by hon. members on the government side of the house during the resolution stage preceding this bill, I would say that the bill does not bear out in full the ideas expressed by those hon. members; and perhaps the banking and commerce committee, as I indicated, would be the proper place to sound out their views and attempt to draft a much better and more expansive bill than we have at the present time.
My suggestion that this bill be referred to the banking and commerce committee is not an attempt to indicate that this is not an emergent situation and that the economy does not warrant some sort of activity of this kind. Obviously the minister himself is not as concerned about having this bill advanced through the house and finally becoming statute law as quickly as was indicated in the speech from the throne, because one of the conditions in the bill is that-and I am not going into the details-it will come into force 90205-6-17
upon proclamation, which could indicate some sort of indefinite time in the future.
If the minister and his colleagues were desirous of this particular bill becoming law as quickly as possible, then the words "upon proclamation" would not have been in there; the bill would have been debated and dealt with here and sent to the Senate for its consideration and given royal assent immediately upon passage by the Senate. Perhaps this is the course that should be taken.

The minister cannot have it both ways. Either he knows what he is doing and he is prepared to advance the legislation and regulations as quickly as possible, or he is in no great rush and does not want it to proceed in the manner that it should.
Inasmuch as the minister has not any idea what should be in the regulations until proclamation takes place, perhaps the proper thing to do would be to send the bill to the banking and commerce committee so he might get the benefit of the views of the members of that committee, many of whom would be from his own party, in order that the regulations perhaps would be more properly worded in such a way as to advance the cause of small businessmen more than they might if the minister merely drafts them based upon his own knowledge and understanding.
One of the things in the bill which is not too acceptable to us is its restrictive quality, as I see it, confining loans to a type of activity dealing with the improvement or modernization of certain kinds of business premises. Perhaps the bill should contain a provision which would allow a person to borrow money to purchase or enter into a small business rather than restricting him to improving what he already has an interest in. I am sure there are a number of people in this country who at one time or another
256	HOUSE OF
Guarantee of Loans to Small Businesses have been engaged in small business enterprises and who, if the statistics on bankruptcies are any indication, have gone out of business for a number of reasons. Incidentally, the number of bankruptcies has been increasing since this government took office. Undoubtedly there are a number of people who unfortunately went bankrupt and would like to get into business again. I think they should be given an opportunity to enter into a business under this type of legislation.
This is not a new idea, because the principle of allowing someone to enter into a business with a government loan has been established under the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act, and I should like to make a short reference to that act to indicate that the situations are comparable. The Fisheries Improvement Loans Act provides that a loan can be made by the government for the purchase or construction of a fishing vessel or the purchase or construction of fishing equipment. There is another provision of the act setting forth that a fisherman is one who is interested in a weir or a fishing vessel, or desires to have an interest in one or to purchase one. I think the same principle could be applied under this legislation rather than restricting it wholly to improvement and modernization.
When this legislation becomes law I think it might also be advantageous if provision were made for people to be able to borrow money for the purpose of retiring a mortgage. I imagine there are many businessmen Who have gone into debt in one way or another in recent years and who have found that the interest rate on their debt is rather high. They might find it advantageous to be able to borrow money under this legislation in order to retire the old debt and improve their over-all financial position.
I understand that the Minister of Finance borrowed a few million dollars the other day, or perhaps it was today, in order to retire previous outstanding loans. He borrows money regularly to pay off past debts hoping, I believe, to improve the financial condition of the treasury. Surely small businessmen should be given the same oportunity to engage in that sort of activity. Surely they should be able to attempt to improve their financial lot by borrowings of one sort in order to pay off borrowings of another kind if they believe they will benefit by the alteration.
We also find it odd that no limit is stipulated in the bill with respect to interest rates. It is odd from our point of view, because if the government is to guarantee these loans I think we are entitled to come to the conclusion that the implication is that


there is practically no risk involved in making such loans. If the operations under the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act and the Farm Improvement Loans Act are any indication, bad debts are a relatively small fraction of the total amount of loans made by the banks, and these losses are guaranteed.
To all intents and purposes it can be said that there will be no risk in lending money to small businessmen under this legislation when it becomes law. As there is no risk, as there is a money-back guarantee on the part of the Minister of Finance, certainly the interest rate should be somewhat lower than is the general case. I think pegging the interest rate at 5 per cent, as was done under the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act, would be the equitable thing to do rather than leaving the situation wide open and allowing the interest rate to be at the same level as the prime interest rate in the case of other people. The fact that to all intents and purposes there is no risk involved is all the more reason why this should be done.
I will have other comments to make at the committee stage of the bill, at which time I will go into more detail with respect to some of the ideas I have now put forward in general terms.

Guarantee of Loans to Small Businesses
was a measure which was inimical to small business. Surely the government has shown, as a result of all the legislation it has introduced and the actions it has taken, that here at long last is a government dedicated to the preservation and the advancement of small business and the little people of the country. I do not want to go into detail on that. All one has to do is make a casual survey of the legislation which has been passed since 1957. Last year we had amendments to the Combines Investigation Act. We had the bill of rights. We have also had many other measures, financial and otherwise, for the benefit and assistance of the small family farmer.
These are but a few of the many important measures which indicate beyond any doubt that the government has taken a firm stand with respect to this question and in doing so has reversed what I can only describe as the cult of bigness which, unfortunately for this country, characterized the last administration for so many years, a cult of bigness in government and bigness in business.
The act now before us is just one of the measures which will achieve the change in this philosophy which clearly indicate the pattern that has been emerging for three years, and which are proof of the fact that the government stands firmly on the side of and behind the small people of this country.
The hon. member for Burin-Burgeo spoke also on the resolution stage, and I was very interested in hearing him refer to what I heard described for the first time as the Pearson plan, which probably indicates an attempt to merge the rather tattered shreds of the Liberal party within the more robust standards of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson).

The facilities of the industrial development bank should be extended to include retail trade. It is essential that our small merchants should have the opportunity to raise capital on reasonable terms.
There are these distinctions, quite plain and quite palpable. It would invoke the machinery of the industrial development bank, which has many inherent weaknesses and certainly could 90205-6-17J
not do the job which this legislation is designed to do. There would be the firm distinction in the amount of capital available. Then, third, the suggestions contained in the Pearson plan are restricted to the retail trade. On the contrary, in this bill I am not going to go into this in any detail because obviously during the committee stage there will be an opportunity to do so. Finally, the main distinction is and I think this is very important, that the Pearson plan was, in the words of the quotation to which the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter) referred on page 57, merely an election campaign plan. He said:
-I should like to quote from page 22 of the Pearson plan, which our leader put forward when the 1958 election was called.
Obviously this bill now introduced is not an election plan but a firm piece of legislation containing the obvious benefits for which this country has been waiting and which will serve a most useful purpose.
I do not want to take up too much of the time of the house, Mr. Speaker. I know there are others who want the opportunity to say something about this particular bill. However, I think I should add this: This legislation can be used in connection with other complementary acts as an instrument of national policy. I say this because I come from a constituency which is remote from the settled areas of Canada, and for many years we have been restricted almost exclusively to agricultural production. During the last 10 or 15 years there has been a slow and gradual change, much of which I should say has been accelerated by the program which this government has commenced during the last three years to the effect that we should now turn our attention to diversification. In this way, we could fulfil our great destiny.
We have in our country a great potential for agricultural development, with gas and oil resources, lumber, minerals, fisheries and so on. We are now at the stage where we may expect industrial development and secondary industries. We have been held back because of the lack of capital. The provisions of this legislation can be used, as suggested by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Woolliams), in connection with the housing legislation, as an instrument of national policy

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while I have listened to a great many interesting speeches in this house for many years, and while I have the highest regard personally for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), I must tell him that I And this bill disappointing. It is disappointing because the bill fails to provide the assistance and the stimulus which small business requires if small business in this country is to continue to survive and to fulfil a very useful economic function in our general economy.
The small businessman has a much greater concern than merely acquiring new plant and equipment. Competition is the vital thing at the moment, and the small businessman is faced with tremendous competition from the large chain stores, large chain retail outlets, which are obviously reducing his margin of profit considerably. There is no doubt that the gross profits of small businesses are shrinking. There is no doubt that the modern purchasing techniques of chain producers and chain retailers amount to severe competition. The big operators are overshadowing the small. Bankruptcies are up sharply in 1960, and it is almost trite to say that we are in the throes of a merchandising revolution. So I say the small businessman needs credit to keep pace with this competition.
This bill we are discussing today gives no special consideration to any taxation; it gives no chance to acquire working capital. It is the lack of working capital, in my opinion, that is the real problem of the small businessman today. With a reasonable amount of working capital, he could compete and he could survive. With a little financial fat on his bones he could ride out the ups and downs of the economic situation that we have had from time to time in this country. But without this financial fat on his bones he faces bankruptcy, no matter how much credit this bill may pretend to grant him for the increasing of his plant and the purchasing of necessary equipment.
I do not believe anyone in the house has any dispute with regard to the general principle, namely the need of small business for capital, the need to purchase new equipment and, if necessary, to renovate premises. If a guarantee is necessary, if it is required by the banking system, then it is only fitting that the government should provide it. However, it is a rather small gesture, to my way of thinking, toward solving the economic problems of 1960, and those which will face us in 1961.

speechtext: Small business does not think so.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF LOANS TO SMALL BUSINESS ENTERPRISES
speechtext: I doubt very much if the measure will create a large number of jobs in the various supply and manufacturing trades, as it is supposed to do. The government for example, is proposing to guarantee a loan by the same yardstick which the banks apply at the present time. I say that this is no basic solution for the chronic problem, the shortage of working capital which faces the small businessman. I say, further, that this bill is disappointing because we have been promised so much over the last three years. In the 1957 election and the 1958 election representatives from the other side of the house went across the country promising to establish an office in the Department of Trade and Commerce to assist small business financially. I believe they did it; I believe they did open up one office. They did put one person in charge, appoint an officer. They did give that one person in that one office a secretary.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: Surely you know it is much more than that.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF LOANS TO SMALL BUSINESS ENTERPRISES
speechtext:
I should like very much to hear the details about that particular office and what it has done in the last three and a half years that we have been waiting for this bill to come forward. I understand that in July, 1960 two deputy ministers were appointed. Again I assume that one of them was charged with the job of investigating now small business could be helped. At long last, on November 22, my friend the Minister of Finance brings in this bill rather than the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees). I suppose we should congratulate him on the action he has taken in at least bringing in this bill. However, I think we must criticize the government for its three and one half years of delay and for the long time it took in presenting legislation in the form in which we have it today because it does not attack the root problem of the small businessman.
It is obvious that the small businessman deserves all the help that we can give him. The present bill may help him in acquiring new machinery, in building a new plant and in making his premises more attractive, something which should help in the retail section of the economy. However the operators of these businesses and the communities which they serve will not gain the full benefit of these improvements unless there exists the financial ability to compete and to survive.
If you look at clause 3 (l)(c) of the bill, Mr. Speaker, you will find that the bank officer is to use the same care required by the bank in

the conduct of its ordinary business. This bank official must, I presume, be sure that the person who is applying for the loan has the ability to stay in business and that he has sufficient working capital. If those two restrictions are applied to any borrower who is trying to get money by means of which to improve his premises or to purchase machinery it seems to me that he will be under much the same restriction that he is under at the present time. I therefore do not expect the flood of new applications which various hon. members who have spoken in the house have predicted. Furthermore, the minister must, if he is a good minister, limit to 10 per cent the guarantee to the banks which in turn will form another check on the granting of loans and the creating of employment. I say that the need is much greater than this.
It seems to me that today there are at least three present needs for small businesses. There is first of all the need of access to equity financing. By that I simply mean that the small businessman first of all starts with his own resources. Then if he needs more money he turns to his friends and to his relatives. When the money from these sources dries up he has no place to which to go. He is too small for the general money market. He cannot go and raise stock issues and bond issues. He has not the necessary security, name, experience or the business. The present basis of taxation which we have in this country does not permit him to accumulate the capital he needs. I say that the second need of the small businessman is for long term debt financing. Too many small owners of small enterprises who have started in good faith and have set up their various businesses in this country and who need money for expansion and capital requirements in due course find themselves the employees of those who advance the money and find that they have lost control of the companies which they themselves had started. If the operator is clear of long term debt or if the debt which he has is of a small amount he may-and I underline the word "may"- qualify for a loan under this bill.
The third need to which I would call the attention of the house is the need of the small businessman for a revision of taxation rates. The small businessman needs a better break on his early profits. Today he is taxed at the same rate as are the larger companies. I submit to the Minister of Finance that the real problem of the small businessman can be solved more readily by a program of tax relief and concessions. This bill offers a small businessman no more or no less than the assistance which the government at present offers to the home owner, the farmer and the fisherman. The small businessman needs much more than that. When the Minister of Finance
Guarantee of Loans to Small Businesses brings down his baby budget before Christmas I hope he will consider giving some tax relief and concessions to the small businessman. If I may, I should like to suggest the following tax relief and concessions which the minister might consider.

Yes; it will just be postponed a year and a half or so. In any event, if I may, I should like to call the attention of the minister to the basic question as it affects small industries and it is this. The rate of depreciation is far too low at the present time. As the minister well knows, the rate of depreciation is 20 per cent the first year. I maintain that it should be increased up to 50 per cent at least the first year and the balance within another year or two. I would also suggest that instead of granting loans up to a maximum of $25,000 the minister should perhaps give tax relief up to the amount of $25,000 in consideration of the necessity for the small businessman to acquire working capital.
If those steps were taken by the Minister of Finance I believe that, in combination with the terms of the bill as we have it at the present time, an approach at least would be made to the root of this problem; that a contribution would be made to the stability and the financial welfare of that sector of the economy which we designate as small business and that this would be done without placing an undue strain on the national treasury.
Other hon. members have mentioned the industrial development bank. I assume the minister has looked at the industrial development bank in relation to the bill. As far as I am concerned, I feel that we should expand the operations of the industrial development bank. I think it is far too conservative. Although I understand its terms of reference provide for loans to industrial enterprises-that is to say to producers and to manufacturers but not to retailers-at the present time it seems to me that it is just a subsidiary of the Bank of Canada. The staff of the bank look to the Bank of Canada and I think the industrial development bank is run in much the same spirit as is the Bank

Guarantee of Loans to Small Businesses of Canada. I think the time may have come when the industrial development bank should be separated from the Bank of Canada. I think the time has come to modernize it, to make it more aggressive, to induce the bank to take more and greater risks and to seek out small businesses which it certainly could help.
In closing I should like to suggest a few things to the Minister of Finance. First, I should like to suggest that he give consideration to placing the administration of the proposed legislation under the jurisdiction of the industrial development bank. I appreciate that this action might require changes in the bill that is before us and perhaps changes in the charter of the industrial development bank itself. However, I think this step would certainly be worth while. My suggestion is that the industrial development bank become the agency of the government in this matter working with the chartered banks which would deal with the applications and make any authorized loans. There is a gap in existing credit facilities for small business in Canada. I hope this bill is no mere political subsidy for one segment of the community but rather is a real attempt to underpin small business enterprise.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity of saying a few words on this bill which is now before the house. Many fine contributions were made by many members on this side of the house during the resolution stage, and I was surprised at the very few remarks we heard from those on the opposite side of the house. The two hon. members who have spoken on this bill regarding loans to small business both seemed to be following along the same line of thought. They spoke of small business needing credit and needing working capital. Do they not realize that this very bill which we have proposed and which is now before the house is here just to do that? What it means is that a man in business, rather than tying up his money in capital expenditures and in other forms of operation, can now obtain a loan to improve his property and increase his efficiency. He can do this, and not tie up as much capital in those fields.
They spoke of what this party has done to help the small businessman. I think both hon. members-the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. Macnaughton) and the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter)-can, if they want to, go up and down the streets in their communities and ask the retail merchants and those in small business what they think of this bill which is now before the house. They would get nothing but glowing remarks and fine praise for what this government has done. They know there are many


small businesses in their communities that require and would like these loans made available to them.
They ask, what have we done, as a party, for small business? Have they forgotten the time of the tight money days? Just ask some of the men in small business about those days of tight money. And do they remember the time when they elbowed the small businessman out of business by doing away with the Resale Price Maintenance Act in 1951? Ask the businessman what he thinks about that. Ask him what he thinks about the Conservative party and its efforts to reintroduce amendments to the Resale Price Maintenance Act, as we did last session.
Therefore I think if they would both earnestly ask themselves about this bill they would come forward and say they are in accord with the measure which we have now placed before the house. Yes, Mr. Speaker, I am very proud to be a member of the government which has seen the problem that exists and has done something about it. We did not turn a deaf ear to these serious problems.
However, I do not think I should take the time of the house to elaborate on the plight of small business. Every member of this house knows full well the situation, if he has the interests of his constituency at heart. He knows that the number of businesses-and they are not all small businesses either

that are struggling for existence because of the lack of capital to enable them to be more competitive is very great.
Every hon. member knows that these small businesses are the lifeblood of any community. These men take part in civic affairs and community interests. They take part in Red Cross canvassing and all these efforts that go on in any community. Who is it gets behind and promotes these things? It is the small businessman in the community. In many cases their forefathers in these small businesses have been pioneers of the country. They helped to develop all these cities in Canada

and what for? For chain stores to come in and take over.
Apart from setting up the industrial development bank in 1944 the Liberal party did nothing for the small businessman. They forgot him. If anything, they put him out of business; they put him out of his place in our economy. Yes, Mr. Speaker, they gave the small businessman a real push out of business in 1951 through the Liberal legislation that abolished the system of resale price maintenance. We went about bringing these back into focus.
I will now proceed with some remarks concerning this bill. Mr. Speaker, I think

it is only natural that loans should be made available to small business as well as farmers, manufacturers and others. The geographical situation of Canada in itself makes it necessary that we should help develop small business because 44 per cent of our population is to be found adjacent to the communities of 1,000 or less, while there are only 40 places where the population is 30,000 or over.
If retail stores had not followed the settlers we would not be the nation that we are today. How many small business concerns are likely to need assistance? This is rather difficult to say or to forecast, Mr. Speaker; but according to Dunn's Review and Modern Industry of October, 1957, a survey of a crosssection of industry in the United States revealed these figures: 9.6 per cent of the retailers, 9 per cent of the wholesalers, 12.4 per cent of the manufacturers and 14.1 per cent of the service establishments were being held back in their growth by lack of capital and financing.
Applying these percentages to the following Canadian figures, we find that retailers total 151,626; and using the 9.6 per cent figure for the United States of those needing assistance, we find we would have 14,566 retailers needing capital assistance in Canada.
Likewise with wholesalers the figure is 26,167; and using the 9 per cent figure for the United States, we find that 2,355 would need assistance in Canada. With regard to manufacturers the figure is 37,021; using the 12.4 per cent figure for the United States, 4,590 would need assistance in Canada.
Finally, in the service establishments the figure is 58,748 in Canada; using the 14.1 per cent figure for the United States there would be 8,283 needing assistance in Canada. We find that 10.89 per cent of the total of these four groups may need financial assistance. If we eliminate manufacturers, who have access to the industrial development bank, there would be some 25,000 prospects for these loans set forth in Bill No. C-40.
Is a loan of $25,000 sufficient? Yes, I think this is a very reasonable maximum. The small business administration act of the United States reports that 51 per cent of the loans they made were for $25,000 and under. In a three-year period that same organization- the small business administration of the United States-made 2,316 loans to wholesale, retail and service establishments for $72,777,136, or an average of $31,424. Therefore in Canada they estimate that for a hardware store 10 per cent of last year's gross would be a reasonable figure to use for remodelling or fixing up a store.
A Canadian grocery survey of a short time ago stated that a grocer who wishes to modernize his store with refrigeration for
Guarantee of Loans to Small Businesses frozen foods, meats, etc., in the hope of meeting competition of the big chains, requires from $25,000 to $75,000, with an average of $27,500.
I think the amount of $25,000 is a very fair maximum. If a merchant or small business operator takes a loan of $10,000 it will mean that over a period of 10 years he will have $1,000 a year to repay on principal or approximately $83 per month or $20 per week. This should not impose too much of a drain or hardship on almost any small operation.
Will the $250,000 gross revenue or sales make most of those in the four categories, namely retail, wholesale, manufacturing and service industries, eligible for loans under this bill? I think it will. I believe the minister in his remarks drew attention to a survey made in 1957 which indicated that 95 per cent of the retail stores had a gross revenue of $200,000 or less-which would take care of practically all the retail houses-57.3 per cent of the wholesalers had a gross revenue of $200,000 or less and 74.6 per cent of the manufacturers had a gross revenue of that amount or less. I therefore think almost all those in small business will be covered adequately.
Bringing this matter home to our own constituencies or our own backyards, as it were, I think of the benefits that will accrue to many engaged in small businesses. I think of the old established family business handed down from father to son with a new generation coming along with the business needing a loan so it may be revitalized. I think of the many new Canadians who have come to Canada some of whom have settled in my own community and built little enterprises that are hamstrung for lack of capital with which to enlarge their premises or improve existing equipment. I think of the corner grocery store in a new area in my constituency. The area has expanded, there has been great development. We want to establish a sub-post office in that area. The grocer wants to put it in his store but does not have sufficient room in his little shop. By getting a loan for building an addition he could have the sub-post office thereby satisfying a need in that community.
I think also of the jewellery store operator who wishes to install a new store front. I think of the main streets of the small towns where the store fronts may need renewing. Of what great assistance it will be to those small communities to have their main streets brightened up with new store fronts.
I think of small manufacturing concerns perhaps operated by new Canadians who have come to Canada and brought with them their

Guarantee of Loans to Small Businesses trades. Perhaps they have a wonderful business that is growing by leaps and bounds but they have not adequate room in which to carry on their work efficiently. These loans will be just made to order for people in that position.
I think of a fruit wholesaler who has worked up a nice business and who needs to instal refrigeration to take care of additional perishable products. He will be able to instal the required refrigeration by making use of the loans instituted by this government. I think of barber shops wanting to remodel, fix up and brighten up. I think of small motels in the tourist area throughout the country and of what great help these loans will be to them. Nor must we forget about the winter works program and of what great assistance this bill will be in developing it, thereby putting more people to work this winter.
All of the people I mentioned and many more will benefit by the passage of this measure, Bill No. C-40. In addition to that I think of the psychological effect its passage will have on those people who are in business and who may never have entertained the thought of securing a loan. When they realize that loans are available many will decide they should take advantage of this opportunity of injecting new life into their business and better business establishments will be the result.
This legislation should go a long way toward fulfilling the request for assistance that has been made by that group of Canadian citizens who operate thousands of small business enterprises throughout Canada, those people who are the mainstay of free enterprise. If the Conservatives and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees) had not listened to their legitimate requests for loans to small business the small business operators might easily have been elbowed out of existence altogether.
I do not believe it is necessary for me to say again how necessary it is to keep the efficient, independent merchant in a strong position. This is in the consumers' long term interest. Any legislation is only as successful as the number of times it is used. I would therefore strongly urge that this bill be enacted as quickly as possible. As soon as the Christmas rush is over small businesses and particularly retailers will turn their thoughts to remodelling, fixing up and making improvements on their premises. The sooner this measure is enacted the better. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) should find this measure of great assistance in stimulating his winter works program as I mentioned before.


I would hope that the chartered banks and more particularly the local bank managers will get behind this loan scheme and make loans available to the small competent businesses with creditable records for meeting their obligations. There are many of them in every community and they are making a very worthwhile contribution.
The retail merchants association, the wholesalers association, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, the tourist industry and others will, I know, all get behind this measure and go all out to inform their members and others about the availability of loans when this bill has been passed.
In my opinion this is one of the finest pieces of legislation to help small business that has ever been introduced. Hon. members opposite have said that this measure does not provide enough assistance, that it does not do this and does not do that, but they have not advanced any better suggestion. I must remind them that they were in power for many years during which time they had the same opportunities to introduce legislation of the type that is now before the house.
