Mr. Speaker, while I spoke for a few moments at the resolution stages, as hon. members of this group are particularly interested in the development and protection of socially desirable legitimate free enterprise and the economic family farm unit as necessary segments in a democratic society performing a useful function because of their economic and social impact upon our society as such, I return to the subject once again as a small boy does to a good fishing pool.
We support this bill in principle although, as the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) mentioned when speaking, we think it is restricted in some respects and in discussion at the committee stage we intend to introduce a few amendments with a view to improving the legislation.
The development of monopoly control in business has been recognized in this country by many groups and individuals over the years with its consequent effect on small business and the economic family farm unit. On that account this group has urged the governments of the day to introduce legislation of this principle and type.
We are very pleased to see that the government has finally responded to the pleas of persons inside and outside of this house and has brought in this legislation. In addition to that, members of the Retail Merchants Association of Canada, representatives of small industries in Canada, and other groups, have made representations to the government, particularly in recent years, urging legislation to

provide some medium or long term credit for their use in the development and expansion of their business.
I want to read briefly from a pamphlet which came to my desk some time ago entitled "Free Enterprise for Small Businessmen". I want to read from page three because I think this case is very well stated. I agree with what is said in this paragraph; I think most members will. It is headed:
Freedom of Opportunity Should be Cardinal Principle of Combines Legislation
It is our principal contention that, under present circumstances, some of the basic principles of our democratic and free society should be restated and re-emphasized.
We can agree with that. I continue:
Because of the disparity in economic power between large and small business, it is necessary for public policy and legislation to protect small business and to strengthen it against the ever present attempts of large business to assert effective control over it.
How true that is.
If economic freedom is to continue to have practical meaning in Canadian society, independent businessmen must be left free to make their own decisions as to sources of supply, pricing and other business policies and not be subject to the dictation, direct or indirect, of large organizations on these matters vital to the operation of their businesses.
This pamphlet was in a brief submitted to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton), in 1959. No doubt the gentlemen who wrote this pamphlet felt keenly the impact of the indirect or direct control of big business on their operations.
I want to say this before proceeding. It is interesting to note this development in the outlook of small business with respect to our society. Not so many years ago you heard the small businessman say that he wanted freedom; he did not ask for any government action, any government attention or any government intrusion into business. Today we have the government accepting the principle which has been advocated by this small and staunch group throughout the years, that government must give leadership in many of these problems. Here we have the government today by this legislation-and rightly so -giving leadership to protect legitimate free enterprise and its interest in this country.
Members of this group and various organizations that I have mentioned made representations for some years urging legislation along the lines that is being discussed by the house at the present time. What was the result? Well, finally, the former Liberal government recognized the problem of small business to a very minuscule extent by the publication of a small business manual. Then, later on, after this government came 90205-6-18
Guarantee of Loans to Small Businesses into power, the problem was further recognized by the establishment of a small business branch in the Department of Trade and Commerce. Therefore, there was some limited recognition of the need for some consideration of the problems of small business.
What was this manual that the Liberal government distributed? Really it is a most enlightening document, Mr. Speaker, if hon. members would only read it. It is a sort of junior business primer. I think it would be normally sent to a high school student who was contemplating the establishment of a peanut vending stand, or something of that sort. However, there is some useful information in it; I would say, after reading the pamphlet through, that it takes a very, shall I say, elementary view of the problems of small business and rather underestimates the intelligence of those who would be establishing small business in this country. It deals with the law and regulations, and that is very useful. It deals with government agencies communicating with small business. It is also an elementary text book on forms of ownership, desirable location of factory sites or stores, accounting methods, use and sources of credit, buying and selling on credit, and then last, but not least, it deals with how to go into bankruptcy. It is a masterpiece of simplicity when it comes to a contribution to the solution of the problems of small business. If hon. members have not read it, then I suggest that they do so.
I recommend it to the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Bell), who is now looking in my direction and apparently listening intently. I suggest he read this manual as he will find it will provide a contribution to his store of knowledge and may help him to fulfil to better advantage his duties as parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance.
As I said before, it is a useful document to a person just commencing to engage in business activity, but it was no solution to the problem whatever. This is a problem which is not confined to Canada; it is a problem of capitalism throughout the western world. It is one of the difficulties of capitalism which has been considered in the United States for some years. In fact, in 1956 a committee of the cabinet of the United States made a report on the difficulties of small business and made certain recommendations to remedy the situation. Thinking and progressive people in the United States realize that while we continue to talk about free enterprise, free enterprise is disappearing almost overnight in many sections of our economy.

I heard a voice over to my left but it was so ghostly that I am not going to reply to it.
In addition, there have been many books published on the subject in western Europe, in Great Britain and in the United States particularly, and a few publications, mostly pamphlets, in Canada, as a result of some superficial studies of the question. But it is a problem facing capitalism in the western world, and one that has to be faced if we are to maintain the form of economic democracy. I say that those who support only large companies and those who associate themselves with those ideas, or those who remain inert in the face of, shall I say, continued dissolution of the small sector of our business in this country are simply digging their own graves, and paving the way for some form of dictatorship in the future. That is why we in this group are very concerned about the maintenance of socially desirable, responsible, legitimate free enterprise and the economic family farm unit.
To illustrate the wide range of interest in this problem, even John Buchan, a former governor general of this country, paid some consideration to this question. I want to quote from his book, "Pilgrim's Way", written in 1940, in which he had this to say about the basic dilemma; this is a basic dilemma that faces capitalist society at the present time and I quote from the book:
Somehow or other, we must make our social and economic world more fluid.
He means 'fluid' in the right sense.
We must widen the approaches so that honest ambition and honourable discontent may have elbow room.
The world must remain an oyster for youth to open. If not, youth will cease to be young, and that will be the end of everything.
Let me say this, Mr. Speaker. Because we have allowed this state of affairs to develop, and it is developing at an alarming rate in the forest industry in British Columbia, we have this situation. I tell hon. members now for their information that within the last year one very wealthy United States lumberman has come into my constituency and has acquired practically all the timber in the Slocan circle. He has acquired the mills with the exception of one small one and now has this entire area for a distance of some 20, 30 or 35 miles under his control. The small men who fought for this country, who were born there and have lived there all their lives, are losing their opportunity to go into business in a small way.


Small business, Mr. Speaker, is not always inefficient. There are opportunities in the forest industry for small saw mills and small industry operating in areas in which it is not economical for the large companies to operate. I mention this matter because it is something that is going on daily and I repeat that governments and corporations who allow this sort of thing to develop are digging their own political and economic graves and laying the foundation for some form of dictatorship in the future.
I wish to quote from a book entitled "Small Business and Venture Capital", by Rudolph L. Weissman, published in 1945 in the United States. This is what he has to say:
Once again we must choose. Either we wish to maintain free enterprise, modified in the course of industrial evolution to fit a 20th century one world economy, or we desire to break abruptly with our traditions to embrace a society of big business only, with cartelization and monopoly as accepted features.
That is our choice at the present time. That is the choice that the people of Canada and the other countries of the western world face in the economic field. I am
very happy, Mr. Speaker, to rise this afternoon in support of Bill C-40. Besides, it is a

pleasure for me to speak after one of the socialist leaders. We are in perfect agreement; we have to do our utmost to save free enterprise.
I represent a Quebec constituency which is half rural and half urban and which, in addition to some large industrial plants, contains a great number of small business enterprises which are defined in paragraph (c), section 2 of Bill C-40 as enterprises where manufacturing, wholesale trade, retail trade and service businesses are carried out.
There are, indeed, a great many small saw mills, manufacturing plants and an even greater number of small retail enterprises which are suffering from the hard competition of some large outside concerns.
Therefore, Bill C-40 comes at the right time, and I consider it a complement to the anticombine legislation. As a matter of fact, the anti-combine act is a purely negative one. Bill C-40, on the other hand, is a positive measure which will enable a great number of small businessmen to get the necessary funds to develop their business.
This bill meets a real need in mixed production areas. From my own experience of small businesses, I can say that if, 15 years ago such a bill had been in existence, it would have been a great help.
I am personally in close and almost daily contact with a great number of small businessmen. I know that everybody will commend the passing of this bill which, because of the loans it provides, will make it possible to proceed with improvement projects. It will, more particularly, help put a stop to what I would call the loan shark racket. I have seen a number of businessmen pay interest rates of up to 10 per cent, capitalized, and the borrower often has to pay a rather large commission on the yield of the loan.
Thanks to this new source of available loans, our businessmen will not have to turn to loan sharks any more. Bill C-40 will also put a stop to the doings of the sharpers who sell, on the instalment plan, store equipment at exorbitant prices, to which are added extremely high financing charges.
I am therefore very happy, Mr. Speaker, to support the principle of this bill and at the same time to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) for his very commendable step which will prove beneficial to free enterprise.
A moment ago I heard the member who is apparently spokesman for the official opposition. He was complaining that Bill C-40 did not provide any working capital loans. From
90205-6-184
Guarantee of Loans to Small Businesses my own experience, I may say that if our small businesses lack working capital, it is precisely because they use their working capital to finance improvements. Consequently, the bill now before us exactly meets the present needs. To my mind, it is not up to the state to provide working capital loans. The chartered banks are already there when it comes to those loans. In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I add that this bill, like all human undertakings, may not be perfect. However, I remember that in 1937, the Quebec government set up the Quebec agricultural credit board, an action that saved agriculture in Quebec at the time. Of course it had to be improved, and amended almost every year. Now this legislation, in my opinion, is just as important in its far-reaching consequences as that of the Quebec agricultural credit board and I feel sure that the Canadian nation will welcome it heartily.

Mr. Speaker, I hope it will not be taken amiss if I say a few words about this bill and especially that I will not be charged' with any attempt to delay its passage. I only have a few remarks to make. I may even be thus doing a service to the government, for this afternoon I noticed that the whips were quite busy trying to find speakers.
During the debate on the resolution, before the bill was introduced, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) said that under this legislation the government may guarantee loans made by chartered banks only. He gave as a reason the fact that credit co-operatives and credit unions are strictly under provincial jurisdiction and that it would be a problem to include them here. He added that the federal government is not authorized at this time to set up any form of supervision on loans granted by those organizations.
I agree with the minister, namely that authorizing those organizations to grant loans under this legislation would be a problem. But, Mr. Speaker, what are we here for if not to solve problems that come up and whose solution might be of benefit to the majority of Canadians?
It seems to me that the Minister of Finance, with all the good will he has shown in the past, should by means of discussions with the parties concerned, be able to reach an agreement that would enable our credit unions and the caisses populaires to make loans just like the chartered banks.
Since the purpose of this legislation is to help small businesses it is necessary to give small businessmen the greatest possible

In some areas of our province, as perhaps in other provinces of Canada as well, there are no branches of chartered banks; or else the majority of small businessmen in those areas deal with credit unions, with caisses populaires. The minister will understand that in those circumstances, the people concerned will have to overcome many difficulties. First, they may have to travel long distances to get to the nearest bank, or they may have to discuss their business with someone with whom they do not generally discuss those matters. The minister will surely agree that in such cases the businessman will find himself handicapped and will not find it as easy to secure a loan. Therefore, I feel that those difficulties could be eliminated if credit unions and caisses populaires enjoyed the same treatment as chartered banks as far as those loans are concerned.
May I also take this opportunity, Mr. Speaker, to praise the wonderful job done by our caisses populaires. I know about them, since the head office of the caisses populaires is in Levis, in my own constituency-and I know from experience the significant role they play not only in helping the development of our small industries but also in helping establish new industries.
Quite recently, I had an opportunity to discuss that matter with some officials of the caisses populaires, and they told me that they were ready to help our small businessmen. You remember that, on many occasions, Canadians were urged to invest their savings in Canadian industries. Well, we know that there are large amounts of savings in our caisses populaires.
I think that the minister would be well advised to give those people the opportunity of investing their savings in this assistance scheme for small businesses.
Besides, someone told me a few days ago, that the caisses populaires have granted several million dollars' worth of loans to small businesses. I therefore ask the minister to reconsider his decision in order to enable our caisses populaires and our credit unions to take part in this worth-while project.

Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to delay the house for long, but I should like to associate myself with the other hon. members in this house who have commended the minister and the government for this fine piece of legislation. Our economy is in a state of constant change, and technological developments are compelling us to constantly shift the emphasis of our legislation from one group in our economy to another for the purpose of creating equity in so far as that can be done through government policy.
This legislation recognizes that the time has come when those who are trying to carry on small business operations require some special assistance to place them in a position where they can compete more successfully in these days of immense organization, the development of great corporations, and when our retail business, which once was carried on in the corner grocery store or in the country store, is now in the hands of our large chain corporations. I am not going to say that this development toward largeness is not a good thing. I believe it is a good thing in some respects. At any rate, it is a development in our economy which has come about for various reasons and which is here to stay.
The small business people are finding it difficult to compete with these large organizations, and this government has demonstrated time and again during the three years of their administration that they are particularly interested in the small operator and in helping the small operator to hold his position in our economy. This legislation is very timely and will assist the small businessman in obtaining credit facilities.
This legislation has been compared to the farm improvement loan legislation. As one who has had some knowledge of the workings

of the farm improvement loan legislation, I should like to say that it has performed a wonderful service to the agricultural people in Canada. It has also been of service to the banking interests. The losses under the farm improvement loan operation have been extremely small. Someone told me they amounted to one tenth of one per cent or three tenths of one per cent. I have talked to bankers who are highly pleased with and have been greatly impressed by the success of the farm improvement loan legislation. It makes it possible for farmers who could not otherwise do so to borrow in order to buy improved equipment and to improve their buildings. This legislation is aimed to provide in much the same way assistance for improving buildings and equipment in the case of small business operators.
The opposition have raised points that were not so much objections to this legislation as they were suggestions that it does not go far enough. From opposition members there have been several suggestions that the industrial development bank should be used for the purpose of extending these loans under the proposed legislation. I would submit that the industrial development bank lacks the branches and that they are not situated in such a way that they can get in touch with enough people who are operating small businesses; they are too remote from the operators of small businesses. On the other hand, the chartered banks have branches in almost every part of the country where business is carried on. It therefore seems to me that the chartered banks are the logical people to handle these guaranteed loans to small business.
Other suggestions were made to the effect that the scope of the legislation should be increased so that people could purchase small businesses, so that they could also pay debts and that the legislation should provide loans for working capital. May I say that there is no limit to the extensions that could be made to the legislation. However, to my mind the legislation is good as it stands. I think it goes far enough to do the job it was intended to do. There are complaints that it does not provide for long term debt financing. Possibly it does not do so, but ten years could be considered to be fairly long term financing in the business world today.
There have been some suggestions that assistance could be granted by offering more rapid depreciation rates for income tax purposes and possibly tax concessions. These suggestions really have nothing to do with this matter of improved credit facilities. I would
Guarantee of Loans to Small Businesses repeat that I think the bill in its present form is good. I should like again to congratulate the minister and the government for bringing in this good legislation and I should like to offer my support. It comes at a time when it will no doubt create a good deal of work and work means jobs, something we need in Canada today as much as anything else. I think the legislation is timely, that it is complete and that it will do a good job for the people of Canada. I know that it will be well received in our constituency of Middlesex West.

The organization which represents the retail merchants of Canada had this to say through its general manager:
We are elated, of course, with, your government's bill to legislate government guaranteed loans for small business through the chartered banks. I have communicated our congratulations to the Prime Minister and to the Minister of Finance.
That statement speaks for itself. Speaking personally as one who comes from western Canada, I may say that I myself am elated with this type of legislation because it brings

Many times when we are out in the rural communities and visit the small merchant stores in the small villages these merchants have pointed out to us members of parliament and those people in public service that sometimes they feel that the small businessman in this country had been forgotten. If he was forgotten under the Liberal government for the past 22 years today he is being remembered by a Conservative government which once again is giving dynamic leadership by bringing in this type of legislation.
I also think it would be of some interest to refer to the Retail Merchants Association of Canada brief and to see what they had to say as to what they wanted. In referring to this brief in that regard I would suggest that it supplies some answer to critics who tried to find something wrong with the bill today and who, in my humble opinion, made an extremely bad job of it. This is what the Retail Merchants Association of Canada asked for; and after all, if that is what they wanted there is no reason why this government, which always has its ear to the ground, should not give the merchants what they asked for. This brief which is dated September 8, 1960 states as follows:
We would further suggest that the loans might be arranged through the chartered banks with whatever government guarantee might be necessary, similar to the provisions of the Home Improvement Loans Act.
In other words, the businessman and small merchant wants his loan from the chartered bank. Businessmen and small merchants want to deal with the man in their own community, whether they are dealing with the Bank of Commerce, the Bank of Nova Scotia or the Toronto-Dominion bank. They want to deal with someone with whom they are used to dealing. Probably they attend the same church, or they belong to the same club, and they can sit down together and are able to understand each other's problems in a mutual way.
Therefore I am quite certain that when the Retail Merchants Association of Canada presented its brief to this government and stated that this was what they wanted, they were speaking for the small businessman in the community. I might repeat, Mr. Speaker, that I feel it is commendable in this way; this government has gone a long way in regard to farm improvement loans and loans in connection with agriculture, and now credit is available to assist the small merchant.
I think, also, that too often when we are looking at legislation of this kind we think


of it as being legislated, or brought in yesterday. Let us think of it as of today, because today there is a revolution going on in the retail trade. The small merchant, whether it is the hardware merchant, the general merchant or the groceteria, is up against very keen competition from large enterprises known as chain stores. This legislation is introduced for the purpose of assisting those small merchants to compete against big business. I think that is very important.
It will also help in this way. Today is the age of specialization. We go to the new shopping centres, and in the new shopping centres we see people specializing in various types of business. Whether it is the business of selling ladies' hats, ladies' dresses, or whatever it is, today we have a form of specialization. This legislation will help the businessman to specialize in his field, by giving him credit to carry on his business. It will also help the country and rural merchants to continue to serve the rural districts of western Canada. He, the merchant in small towns, will be able to serve the farmers in his particular area.
Now I come to one particular field which I feel is going to receive great assistance from this legislation. I am referring to the tourist trade. This legislation will help the businessman who is working in tourist development. In that regard, Mr. Speaker, I might take just a moment of time to refer to part of the definition of "business enterprise" set out in this bill. It covers manufacturing, the wholesale trade, the retail trade and service businesses. In that regard, I suppose the way it will fit into the tourist trade is in the retail trade and service businesses.
Only a few days ago I said it was regrettable that in the tourist trade in a place like Banff, Alberta, where there are more than one million people who come to visit the area each and every year through the the east and west gates, in many cases the small businessman who is serving that type of tourist industry

which is sometimes from eastern Canada, and from the United States -has difficulty in obtaining credit for the motel business and tourist business generally. This legislation shows that the government has listened to some recommendations of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, which after all is an organization that does represent freedom of enterprise and business generally in Canada.
I want to refer for a few moments to the Canadian Chamber of Commerce policy declarations of 1960 and 1961. This, again, shows that the government is right in line with

what is needed in business, because these are new policy declarations of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce.
This is dealing with tourist promotion, and I will read from page 43 of this particular pamphlet. If you will bear with me I want to read two or three paragraphs because I do feel they will be appreciated. After all, the tourist trade is one of the largest businesses today in Canada and brings in more new dollars for us to spend. It is the third largest outside of pulp and the wheat industries. Speaking of tourist promotion the Canadian Chamber of Commerce pamphlet on policy declarations says:
The Canadian Chamber of Commerce recognizes the value and importance of the tourist industry which annually attracts to Canada millions of dollars of new wealth and which can and should be developed to produce an expanding market for food, gas and oil, manufactured articles and services. By promoting this industry a number of major objectives can be achieved, including (a)

(b) by inducing Canadians to visit the many attractions of Canada, thereby developing our own tourist vacation and recreational areas, and (c) by fostering better understanding of Canada by visitors from other countries, thus cementing international friendships.
Those are three high aims. Then it goes on:

Of course, in Alberta there are two, Banff and Jasper:
-provincial parks and other areas of scenic, recreational or historical interest by means of advertising, development of highways, tourist accommodation, recreational facilities and by other means to the fullest possible extent. It is important that, in so far as seasonal conditions permit-
I might just digress from my reading for a few moments. One of the big difficulties of businessmen who are engaged in the tourist industry in Banff and Jasper is that the season is so short. Their profits, if any, from the business accrue in the months of June, July, August and probably September. Sometimes September happens to be a bad month and it works out to just about a three and one half month season. Therefore it is very important to these people. That is why they will be encouraged by this legislation. This applies to people who are doing business in the

I will continue for a few moments reading what the Canadian Chamber of Commerce has to say in its policy declarations:
It is important that, in so far as seasonal conditions permit, each of the national parks should develop accommodation and facilities to provide a year-round program of rest and recreation, so that such facilities may be available to all Canadians in the regions in which they live.
I might add this with reference to the seasonal nature of this industry-and I am thinking of the future of a place like Banff particularly, and probably Jasper-Banff particularly could become the playground of western Canada, and probably all Canada, for winter sports and eventually for the world Olympic games. In this last connection the Banff chamber of commerce is making a strong bid at this time. That is the very point the Canadian Chamber of Commerce has endorsed in its latest policy declarations. It has been asking the various governments at various levels to supply credit where credit has never before existed. As I suggested, this party prior to coming into power in 1957-58 mentioned that it would bring in a bill to assist small business. That is exactly what has been done. The government has kept its promise in that regard.
I wish now to deal with another matter relating to small business obtaining loans. In the past it was difficult for small business to finance because long term loans were not readily available through the chartered banks. In many cases, under the provisions of the Bank Act and because of the way the chartered banks operated, loans had to be paid up within one year. In fact, many notes are on a demand basis and the rate of interest is set out. The chartered banks say that when the interest goes up the interest on the demand notes must go up too, the maximum being 6 per cent governed by the Bank Act: However they never reduce interest rates when they obtain money on a lower interest -rate market. This present measure will enable small business to obtain credit just as the farmers can obtain credit under the Farm Improvement Loans Act.
Before resuming my seat I wish to comment on some of the remarks made by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Her-ridge) who participated in the debate this afternoon. It always surprises me to find that when a dynamic measure such as this is introduced by the Conservative government hon. members of the C.C.F. group leap to their feet and say that this has been brought about because they suggested it. They seek to give the impression that they have advocated these measures for the last 22 years.


In answering the remarks of my hon. friend I thought it might be interesting to find out exactly where that group stands with reference to small business and free enterprise by examining some of the statements of the illustrious leaders of that group in the past.
This subject is of special interest to me because I was born and raised in Saskatchewan and lived there until I was almost 30 years of age. I saw the C.C.F. party come into power in that province. I believe that the socialists in this country represented by the C.C.F. drove business out of that province and succeeded in keeping it out. I am thinking about the lumber business for example. I remember that the small lumber yard owner was chased out of Saskatchewan because the C.C.F. government took over the lumber business under the lumber board. The same applies to the fishing industry. The C.C.F. government also took over the shoe manufacturing business and the woollen manufacturing business. In fact, even insurance agents were driven out of the province of Saskatchewan because the C.C.F. government implemented its own insurance scheme. There was no thought about loans to help small business. No thought at all directed to help business in Saskatchewan.
As a result of the actions of the C.C.F. government in that province many people have left Saskatchewan. Many individuals and businesses have gone to Alberta. Some people in Alberta with reference to their own provincial government say that it is a conservative government-with a small "c"-and in some respects I must go along with that because they certainly stand for business.
When the socialists claim this afternoon that they stand for free enterprise and small business I say we should take a look at some of the things that were said by distinguished leaders of that party in the past. I do not know if C.C.F. members today endorse what was said in the past in view of the new party being born, but let us examine what was said by no less distinguished a person than Mr. Coldwell in his maiden speech in this house. By the way, Mr. Cold-well came from Rosetown-Biggar where I was born and raised. I thought the hon. member from Kootenay West would be interested in being reminded of Mr. Coldwell's remarks in respect to free enterprise. Mr. Speaker, during the throne speech debate the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) criticized much of the legislation which is being brought before the House of Commons because he said, and I paraphrase here, so much of the legislation which we are passing and are about to pass depends on the initiative of the municipalities, of the Canadian people and of the provinces. To my way of thinking, Mr. Speaker, he hit the nail on the head. That is one of the fundamental differences between our party and the party that he leads in opposition today. We have faith in the initiative of the Canadian people; we have faith in the initiative of the provinces; we have faith in the initiative of so many of the institutions for which this type of legislation is designed.
This particular legislation is part of our progressive policy of partnership economic expansion. One of the attractive things about the legislation which can be found in the throne speech and in so many of the announcements of the ministers is that the legislation and policies which are being announced will not encumber the actions of future governments with overhead and debt. In many instances they are self-liquidating programs. To my way of thinking this is one of the very essential things about this particular piece of legislation. It is designed to help the small businessman in our country. I ask everybody in this house, no matter in what party, when in the history of Canada has such imaginative legislation been brought before the House of Commons on behalf of small business? All parties and all members must agree and admit that the answer is, never. This is imaginative legislation which is going to get immediately to the places where it should go.
I am not going into the details and examine here on the floor of the House of Commons, how this legislation will help the small businessman in my particular area. The area I represent in this House of Commons is, like so many areas, made up of small businessmen. I will not pinpoint the manner in which this legislation will help. It is self-evident; it is obvious.
The Leader of the Opposition has gone from one end of this country to the other preaching doom and gloom. I have said this before inside and outside the House of Commons. In time of war we have a bipartisan spirit. I would be the last person to say that all discussions in the House of Commons be approached in a bipartisan manner. No one


likes a good political donnybrook any more than I do but when it comes to getting jobs for Canadians I think we should approach this in a bipartisan mood. With the east-west conflict that is going on I think major matters of economics reflecting the honour of this country should be approached in a bipartisan spirit.
Apart from little procedural amendments they talk about and harp on, unless the opposition have what I call substantive amendments to make and substantive things to suggest in a constructive way, they are doing nothing to help this country at home or abroad by spreading this prophesy of doom and gloom.
The hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer), who is not in the house at the present time, said the other night he was sure that things were going to be terrible economically in the months ahead. How was he so sure? Where is his proof? He did not offer those things in a factual, detailed way; he just said he was sure things are going to be bad. The Leader of the Opposition who spreads so much doom and gloom is now spending, I believe, half his time in New York consulting about the United Nations. He thinks the domestic situation is so bad, or so good, apparently, that he has to spend only half his time in the House of Commons. It is a two-way week, half in New York and half in Ottawa. If this legislation was needed before 1957, which I do not think it was, it was needed in 1957, it was needed in 1958, it was needed in 1959 and it was needed in the first half of 1960. During all that time these wise gentlemen with their great imagination have been responsible for the government of this country and at long last, three and one half years after they took office, they bring in something which is almost a precise mirror, as nearly as anything could be applying to two different industries, of an act of parliament that was introduced by a Liberal government as part of its post-war program, an act which was good legislation, which had worked very well and which we certainly hope will work as well in the present circumstances.
However, I have very little doubt that there could be any possible harm in the government accepting the suggestion of the hon. member for Levis. The fact is that if businessmen do not go to the credit unions or the caisses populaires to obtain such loans the suggestion would not be operative and if they did they would presumably do so because it was more to their advantage to do so. If small business does need credit facilities of this kind at the present time I say that the proof of the pudding will become apparent later. In the case of the farm improvement loans nobody knew for sure whether they were going to work. They have worked out exceedingly well but nobody knew for sure beforehand and nobody knows for sure in this instance. We hope that they will and I am sure the legislation will have some good effects.
However, I think we also ought to ask ourselves another question about this legislation and it is this. Is this legislation a part of the government's program to deal with unemployment or is it a part of the government's program to aid small business, because it is possible it might do both? I do not know whether the minister has any notion of safeguarding against this in the regulations because I find nothing in the bill to this effect but it is just as possible that these loans

Guarantee of Loans to Small Businesses may result, In a temporary way at any rate, in a diminution of employment. If these loans are used by small businessmen to finance capital undertakings of a character which reduce the need for labour, that is to say, for labour-saving devices of one kind and another which many small businesses greatly need, the immediate effect of the legislation may well be to reduce employment.
I am not complaining on that account because small businesses obviously have to modernize if they are going to compete in the world in which we live. It is necessary that they should and it is desirable that they should have every opportunity to do so on an equal basis with others. I do not think we should be too sure that the short term effects of the legislation are necessarily going to be productive of very many jobs. I would hope that possibly that might be the case in the manufacturing field to the extent that advantage is taken of this legislation but in other fields it might very well be that the immediate net effect would be that businesses could be modernized, labour saving devices could be introduced and in fact the need for labour immediately would not be so great.
As I say, this is purely a matter of speculation but we should not build exaggerated hopes, which is not in the least to condemn the legislation because I think we feel that, having such a good model, it is good legislation. However, notwithstanding the enthusiasm of the elderly and experienced member for Brome-Missisquoi and the faith which he expressed in the initiative of the government of the province of Quebec, which I found very touching, I think we should not exaggerate what are likely to be the effects of what after all is not the beginning of the millenium for small business or for the econ-nomy of the country but what may prove to be a somewhat useful device, as Mr. Ilsley's legislation of 1944 has proved to be.

speechtext:
This point was dealt with at the resolution stage. Here let me review some of the legislation in this respect in order to put this point in its true setting. We have four statutes that are comparable in nature and purpose in their respective fields with the one now before the committee. They are the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the Veterans Business and Professional Loans Act, the home improvement loans sections of the National Housing Act and, fourth, the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. Only one of those statutes makes any provision for government guarantee of loans made by credit unions or caisses populaires and that is the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. It was introduced into that act only when amendments to that act were before the banking and commerce committee in the year 1955. It was not in the original bill introduced in the house. The case made at that time was of a special nature, namely that there were many fishermen in quite remote fishing villages to whom ordinary banking facilities were not available but to whom lending facilities by credit unions were available. That view commended itself at the time both to the banking and commerce committee and to the government and that is the reason why you find provision made today in the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act, in section 2 (j), that the word "lender" in the act means:
(i)	a bank, and
(ii)	a credit union, caisse populaire, or other co-operative credit society designated by the minister as a lender for the purposes of this act;
In none of these other statutes were caisses populaires or credit unions admitted to the benefit of the act. Provision for them is not found in the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the Veterans Business and Professional Loans Act or in the home improvement loans sections of the National Housing Act. What is the reason? I think the reason is simple. The banks are federal institutions; they are under 

the control of parliament in all respects. In the way they transact their business they are subject to federal supervision. Then the interest rates which the banks charge are governed by legislation of this parliament. In the case of credit unions or caisses populaires, these are provincial institutions. In no respect are they subject to federal jurisdiction or federal supervision and they are under no limit as regards the interest rates which they may charge so far as the legislation of parliament is concerned.
Bearing this in mind, Mr. Chairman, may I say that, if we make the kind of amendment which the hon. member for Laurier is trying to work into this bill tonight we would be committing ourselves to guaranteed loans at whatever interest rates the caisse populaire or credit union might charge. There is no percentage limit imposed by law on them. Already in the course of discussion at the resolution stage we had testimony from hon. members of this House of Commons who have had experience in this field of lending through credit unions and caisses populaires and they pointed out that the interest rates charged by these institutions are in many cases substantially above 6 per cent.
These are just a few of the reasons why it is quite inappropriate to introduce into this measure provision for extending government guarantees to loans made by a credit union or caisse populaire. I think it is quite clear to the committee why these institutions were not included and why it would be quite inappropriate to include them. We have had no request from credit unions or caisses populaires for inclusion in the provisions of this act. I wish to make that point quite clear. No doubt if they were invited or stirred up they would probably ask for the benefit of these guarantees. What lending institution would not do so? But the fact is that we are dealing here with small business and the facilities of the branch banking system of this country, with between 4,000 and 5,000 branches, are available to small business.
Effective supervision can be carried out in the operations of these institutions under the federal legislation existing for the purpose. This does not imply any antipathy towards caisses populaires or credit unions; far from it. The fact is, however, that we are a federal parliament. We are legislating in the federal sphere. The caisse populaire and the credit union are within the provincial sphere. It would be perfectly proper for provincial parliaments to legislate with respect to those institutions.

I do not think the minister really intends to hold a special brief for the banks over and above other lending institutions and to tell the committee that the banks are government institutions. The banks are privately owned and privately administered lending institutions, the same as are the others. But why we should legislate to give a preference in this business loans act to this particular type of lending institution is far beyond my understanding.
In the national housing legislation we certainly recognize insurance companies, trust companies and a variety of lending institutions. Now it is said that these are provincial matters. Certainly they are subject to control by this parliament as to their interest rates, and they are subject to control by the superintendent of insurance.
Whilst we are legislating in this section we are actually defining the word "bank". If the word "bank" is not already defined in other acts, why then do we particularly say in this act that "bank" shall mean so-and-so? If we are now defining "bank" I think we can extend this definition to all other recognized lending institutions.
I think we would be going far afield to say we will legislate in favour of one type of lending institution. If it is a government institution, it is one thing. But I draw to the minister's attention that they are all under the supervision of the Bank Act, and so are other institutions under that supervision. Certainly these banks are privately owned and controlled, but we should not legislate differently for them and we should not treat them on a different basis than other institutions in the country.

I am sure this has just been overlooked for the moment. I venture to remind the hon. member for Laurier of these facts.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am not as
familiar as the Minister of Finance or the hon. member for Laurier with those historic days when their places were changed, so consequently I cannot appreciate this chit-chat back and forth about what happened 13 or 14 years ago and who did what. In any event, I think that is entirely beside the point.
I gather that the minister gave two basic reasons why credit unions and caisses populaires were not included as lending institutions in this bill in the first instance. The first one-not necessarily in this order of importance-was that the parliament of Canada had no jurisdiction; that caisses populaires and credit unions came under provincial legislative jurisdiction, and consequently we had no authority over them. To this extent it is quite true. Their interest rates are pegged by provincial legislation.
Surely the minister's argument that because credit unions and caisses populaires are established under provincial legislation we can have nothing to do with them is spurious. The parliament of Canada decided some years ago that it had authority to establish both as lending institutions for the purpose of government guaranteed loans. That is precisely what we are asking to do here.
The Minister of Finance supported an amendment to the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act in 1955. The measure went before the banking and commerce committee indicating that the parliament of Canada has already dealt with this matter. Let me read this again. It has already been referred to. It appears in the Statutes of Canada, volume I, 1955. Contrary to what the minister is trying to lead us to believe, the word "lender" in that act means a bank-and a "bank" means a bank to which the Bank Act applies; and the word "lender" also means:
(j) (ii) a credit union, caisse populaire, or other co-operative credit society designated by the minister as a lender for the purposes of this act;

Parliament has already decided the question of jurisdiction. The minister now uses that as an argument to get around the real reason why he does not want to include them in this bill.
The minister gave as another reason for not including them the fact that there was no limit to the interest and that we have no jurisdiction over the interest charged by credit unions. That is probably quite true. The minister on his own initiative introduced this bill with an open end interest rate attached to it so there can be no limit to the interest rate depending on what the Bank Act says. Because the minister wanted an open end interest rate attached he has deprived himself of his own argument. Even without a pegged interest rate if the provision were contained in this bill the minister, having the authority mentioned in the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act, would surely not designate a credit union or caisse populaire which might have an interest rate in excess of that established by the Bank Act. In most cases I know of the interest rate is lower. The saving feature is there.
The minister's question of jurisdiction has already been decided on by the parliament of Canada and enshrined in a provision in the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act so the hon. gentleman cannot argue on that ground. The minister's second point also has no validity. He should have introduced an interest rate.
It is my hope that we will have an opportunity to vote on this amendment, that the minister will forget his affection for history and forgive himself for making these invalid arguments, admit that he was in error, accept a good point well made and recognize caisses populaires and credit unions as lending institutions under this bill.

I do not know how much time the minister has spent in the fishing communities on the coasts of this country but I do know that I have never yet visited a fishing settlement where three or four fishermen were gathered together that was so very small or remote
Guarantee of Loans to Small Businesses that in the same place there was not a businessman and on the minister's own showing if what was done in the case of the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act was justified and if the government means business in helping small business, these are precisely the kind of people that ought to have this sort of thing available to them, the small businessman in the coves of Newfoundland, for example. Of course, I cannot believe that a great constitutional authority like the Minister of Finance who must have read the British North America Act at Osgoode Hall if he has never looked at it since would seriously argue for one moment that any provincial legislature has any jurisdiction over interest whatever. The minister knows too much for that. He knows that it is one of the specified powers given to this parliament in the British North America Act. The hon. gentleman also knows, as the hon. member for Skeena pointed out, that if the minister wants to prescribe a limit beyond which the caisses populaires or the banks cannot charge interest, it is perfectly competent for him to suggest it and it is perfectly competent for this parliament, if in its wisdom it wants to do so, to do it. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am one of
those who has great confidence in credit unions by virtue of the fact that I helped to organize one and managed it for four years. It has grown into a good sized institution. From a start with $260 it has now over $100,000 and is serving the community.
First of all, Mr. Chairman, I feel that members of credit unions would resent it if they were called lending institutions. We in Manitoba in particular consider them societies for mutual assistance by people who have some common interests. Credit unions are organized by parishes; that is, where membership is restricted to members of that particular parish they are organized as a religious body. Some credit unions are organized on a professional basis, and admit only members of a certain profession. For example, there are branches of credit unions to which only school teachers belong; there are those who work in packing plants; and there are those who work in stores. These various groups of people organize themselves into a credit union; they pool their resources. Then if they have need they go to this institution and draw out money. That is the purpose of the credit union. I do not consider it in the same sense as a lending institution or as a bank.
We have credit institutions which foster co-operatives. If for no other reason than that I am against the amendment. Even if the amendment is in order, Mr. Chairman, I shall vote against it because I think the principle of it is wrong. First of all, the credit unions do not think it a favour to them to be championing their cause in this way. Second, those in particular who are sponsored by or sponsoring co-operative stores or mercantile institutions. They are in direct competition and conflict with private enterprise, private individuals, free enterprise, small manufacturers and other small business to whom I believe it is the intention that this bill will give help. To include credit unions in this bill I think would be ridiculous.
Credit unions are organized for their members. I have yet to hear of small businessmen organizing a credit union of their own for mutual help. They are individualists who
Guarantee of Loans to Small Businesses cut each others' throats in this competition that they have to carry on in order to make their living.
I have another reason why I do not think this is the proper place for the credit union to be classed as a lending institution and come under this bill. The moneys provided by this bill are intended to go out on long term loans. I know that from my own experience. The credit union creates a revolving fund from which short term loans can be made even without security to any member of the credit union who is in need because the character of the individual member is the most important thing so far as these institutions are concerned. How do you relate that to the work of the banks and what the banks expect to achieve?
There is a third reason why we would be doing the credit unions a disservice. Are you going to limit their rate of interest? They are governed by provincial statutes. I cannot speak for other credit unions because I am not familiar with them but every credit union in Manitoba has a charter of its own and bylaws of its own. Each member has one vote only and his savings are insured. If he has $2,000 in savings in the credit union then in the event of his death he has insurance amounting to $2,000. The borrowers are also insured. Any person must be a member to borrow from the credit union and storekeepers and small businessmen might not always be welcome. In the event of the death of the borrower the insurance company pays his debt. The debt is wiped out and his estate is cleared.
Consequently the credit unions charge a high rate of interest. The lowest rate of interest in my own credit union is 8 per cent and in the neighbouring credit union the interest rate is 12 per cent, $1 per month per $100. Even if the credit union accepted the storekeeper as a member how could they work out the interest rate to be charged by the credit union? I think the suggestion that has been made is just a case of imagination on the part of some members who wish to climb on the bandwagon and say "me too". All we have had from them since 1944 is imagination.
I am not making these remarks just for the purpose of hearing myself speak or having the committee hear me speak. 1 honestly feel that the credit unions would not be in favour of this proposal. It would not help their business at all. I do not think it would be accepted and therefore I will vote against the amendment.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to support the proposition that the government should give credit unions and caisses populaires exactly the same kind of guarantee

The hon. member for Marquette said that he doubted whether the credit unions would want this kind of guarantee. I should like to see this measure sent to the banking and commerce committee, not for the purpose of delay but for the purpose of bringing before that committee competent witnesses from the credit unions, the caisses populaires and other interested organizations including the retail merchants association and others in order to find out whether they would like this guarantee provided to credit unions in view of the fact that many of these associations appeared before the banking and commerce committee in 1955 and asked the government that this be done.
I am making a plea that this guarantee be provided to the credit unions because what has happened in the last number of years is that the credit unions and the caisses populaires have been the only source of intermediate credit for small businesses in many communities. I know many businessmen personally who could not obtain long term loans for the renovation of their business premises from the chartered banks. They went to the credit unions of which they were members in their own communities and received loans to enable them to expand their premises and improve their businesses.
As a matter of fact, the credit unions and the caisses populaires have pioneered in this field. It is the banks that have failed and because of the failure of the banks and the desire for credit by small businessmen the government at long last is moving in this direction. However, as the bill now stands it is loaded in favour of the banks and against the credit unions. It definitely discriminates against the credit unions which have pioneered in this field.
I do not know how loud the voices of the credit unions have been in speaking to the minister or whether they have spoken to him at all but I can imagine that the banks would speak with very loud voices in opposing this kind of guarantee being given to credit unions because in many communities the banks are terrified as a result of the tremendous loss of business to credit unions that they considered to be theirs.
The credit unions and caisses populaires are not simply a handful of organizations scattered in a few communities across this country. I have in my hands statistics as to the number of chartered banks in Canada in 1958 and I find that there were 4,677 branches


of chartered banks. In 1958 chartered credit unions numbered 4,485, within 200 of the number of branches of chartered banks.

It shows that the credit unions have great popular support and the government should not discriminate against credit unions by leaving them out of this legislation.
The minister puts forward a number of reasons why he claims it would be inappropriate to provide this kind of guarantee to credit unions. He says there is no supervision by the federal government of credit unions and caisses popularies. I ask the minister: Is there any supervision whatsoever by the federal government of the credit unions that have provided loans to fishermen under the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act? Does the minister mean to imply that the credit unions and caisses popularies are not sound businesses, that the federal government must supervise them in order to provide the guarantee? I do not have the information-perhaps the minister has-but I will venture to say that the rate of collection of small loans with comparable risks is much better for the credit unions than for the chartered banks. Yet the government is providing a guarantee to the chartered banks and refuses to provide the same guarantee to credit unions.
The minister says that it is not in other acts. Because a mistake has been made in the past is no reason to continue the mistake today. I have certainly advocated on former occasions that guarantees given to the banks in other acts should be applied to credit unions.
The Minister of Finance says that the hon. member for Laurier and the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate are shedding crocodile tears for the credit unions and caisses populaires but in at least one act the former administration did the right thing. This government has yet to do the right thing in the first such legislation it has introduced since taking office by providing this kind of guarantee to credit unions.
The minister says that the interest rates of credit unions are higher and therefore the guarantee cannot be applied. Surely the minister is not advancing that as a sound argument. If he is one would think that he has not read, although I am sure he has, the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. It defines

a lender as including a credit union and then it goes on to say that the rate of interest charged by the lender on the loan shall not exceed 5 per cent per annum simple interest In other words, the government can give a guarantee. It can give a guarantee to a credit union, and it can say to the credit union, you can get a guarantee if you do not charge more than 6 per cent interest.
Why does the government not give to the credit union exactly the same kind of guarantee that it is giving to the banks? I plead with the minister that the government give the same kind of treatment to the credit unions which it has given to the banks. I suggest that in hundreds upon hundreds of communities across this country the credit union will do better than the banks; credit unions will do a better job, will have better success in collections and will demonstrate to all concerned what a sound, democratically operated small business can do.
I think the government, instead of trying to promote the welfare of the banks in other provisions in this bill should be prepared to give the same kind of guarantee to the credit unions and put them on an equal basis. I am sure that if the minister does not agree with the request today the time will come soon when the credit unions will be recognized by a federal government for what they are, very successful credit institutions. In many communities they are giving a service that is not matched by the banks, and they are providing service in many communities in which banks are non-existent.
I wish the minister would end the discrimination against credit unions and give them a chance to compete on equal terms with the banks.

Mr. Chairman, I followed the discussion which took place this afternoon and tonight very closely. Guarantee of Loans to Small Businesses caisses populaires and our co-operatives in the province of Quebec and throughout the country.
I had the opportunity of going to St. Francis Xavier University, in Antigonish, to study the system of co-operatives and caisses populaires. I was also able to travel about Cape Breton and to study there the caisses populaires system. May I say that I am still wondering who was right, my professors or the opposition members who are discussing the problem tonight.
First of all, the caisses populaires and the co-operatives were established to help certain categories of people in our society. It might indeed be well to remind hon. members that there have been mistakes made in many cases when founding co-operatives. When an attempt was made to establish the system in the cities, for instance, where there was less poverty, the system took a long time to take root, and even now, it can scarcely be said to be successful there.
The system was really of use in places where poverty prevailed. For instance, coal co-operatives were established in Nova Scotia and a caisse populaire was also founded there for the purpose of helping those who were working in the coal mines. The aim of the caisses populaires never was to loan money to industries, but to care for a class of people who have suffered.
Mr. Chairman, that is my answer to the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier), who was asking the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) why he did not want to include the caisses populaires in the bill now before us. To my mind, such attitude would be against the very principle of the caisses populaires which is to look after a certain class of people, and not to make loans to industries.
I therefore commend the government for having taken a similar attitude, because otherwise, it would be working against the very principles of the caisses populaires, and their members would blame their management because they would then be unable to play the part the caisses populaires aim at. That is why I shall vote against the amendment.

Guarantee of Loans to Small Businesses at this time what unfortunate comments perhaps some newsmen will be prone to make concerning the member for Berthier-Maski-nonge-Delanaudiere for rising in this house, apparently to speak against the caisses populaires. That certainly is not my purpose. In my 12 years as a lawyer I have always made it a point to take all my business to those institutions, and I have only praise for all the fine people looking after the financial interests of their members in the various small centres in the province of Quebec.
But, as was so well pointed out by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), those institutions are under provincial jurisdiction and were created by provincial authorities. Going back to section 91 of the British North America Act, subsection 15, we find that banks are under the exclusive jurisdiction of the federal government. First of all, a bank is created through federal legislation. Second, certain administrative regulations under the Bank Act provide that the bank shall set aside a certain percentage of the money at its disposal, to insure sound operations and the security of the people with whom it carries on transactions. The interest rate set by the banks is also controlled by the federal government.
Now, the caisses populaires were created under provincial legislation from which they derive their legal status. Furthermore, their administration is under provincial control. The rate of interest that they are authorized to pay to their members is a matter for the board of directors in each caisse populaire to decide and any loan application must first be submitted to the credit commission.
I fail to see how the hon. member for Laurier, the very man who, last year, was all for respecting the Canadian constitution, can, today, in this house, attempt to treat the caisses populaires like chartered banks, which under section 91 of the B.N.A. Act, are under exclusive federal jurisdiction.
Besides, Mr. Chairman, I wonder what would be the practical effect in the case of those loans which might be granted by the caisses populaires, since, in the province of Quebec, any loan secured by an individual is now automatically insured by the Desjardins life insurance. Thus when a borrower dies while indebted to the caisse, his loan is automatically paid out through an insurance on his loan.
Therefore, I fail to see how, in the discussion of this bill, particularly in clause 3, we could accept the proposed amendment because the purpose of this bill is to pay back


to the banks any amount of money that they might lose if the borrower failed to meet his obligations.
As far as the caisses populaires are concerned this bill is not applicable because, as I said earlier, any loan secured from a caisse populaire is automatically insured through a policy issued by the caisses populaires Desjardins.
